narrative.overview:
ARP is a calm instrument panel for teams that run long agent pipelines and ratify what the agents propose. It reads like a well-kept research report: ink on a cool blue-grey ground, titles and figures in one engineered sans, and every number traceable to the page it came from. One colour, amber, is reserved for one reason only: a person must act. When nothing waits on anyone, no amber appears.

The system is precise and quiet. Cards are flat panels set off by a hairline; Geist carries titles, figures, text and controls, Geist Mono carries IDs and state, and a serif appears only where text is quoted from a source. Density is high enough for tables of thousands of companies while staying legible on a projector. Two themes share one structure: **Night Desk**, in light and dark. The theme switch (System / Light / Dark), in the top bar's user menu, chooses between them, and every component reads its colours from the same tokens.
keyCharacteristics: Blue-grey ground, ink accent for controls (near-black in light, near-white in dark), amber reserved for "waiting on a person".
Status colours (green / amber-brown / red / blue) describe runs and ratings, never the person-must-act state.
Cards are flat: a panel fill and a hairline, no shadow.
Geist for titles, figures and reading; Geist Mono for IDs, labels and state; a serif only for quoted source text.
Three signature elements carry the identity: the Pixel mark language, the needs-you shape and evidence paper.
The start page leads with the five workspaces; everything else is reached from them.

rules.name: The One Signal Rule
rules.body: Amber means one thing only: a person must act. Never use it for branding, decoration, hover, focus of a normal control, or "running". When nothing waits, no amber appears anywhere on the screen. Keyboard focus is an accent outline. A proposed item's box is neutral; only its "Proposed" tag and the needs-you shape carry the signal, so a queue never turns into a wall of amber. The flagged vote that needs a second person takes the signal border.

rules.name: The Brand Colour Rule
rules.body: Brand orange (#ea4c14 light, #ff6a2b Night) appears in two places only: the logo apex and the landing animation's orb glow. It never appears in the app's interface, so it cannot be mistaken for the amber signal.

rules.name: Provenance Is Not Status
rules.body: Where a number came from (live, synthetic sample, portfolio holdings, not built) is shown with neutral marks: filled, half, ring, dashed ring. Metric numbers are ink. Green, amber-brown and red stay for status.

rules.name: The Status Is Not The Signal Rule
rules.body: Status colours describe runs and ratings. Red marks a failed run and also a Low (L) rating on Transition Barriers; that second use is a deliberate, confirmed exception, because the matrix reads as a traffic light. It never marks something waiting on a person.

rules.name: Chart Colours
rules.body: Charts with categories use four slots, `--cat-1` to `--cat-4` (blue, magenta, gold, violet; `lib/palette.ts` explains the validation). They are neither status nor signal.

rules.name: The Arcade Exception
rules.body: The hidden arcade games draw in their own neon palette. They sit outside the product and are the only place where neon is decoration.

rules.name: The Icon Accent Rule
rules.body: Each workspace drawing has exactly one element that can light up: in the signal colour (`--hi`) when the workspace waits on someone, in the running colour (`--run`) when it runs. Otherwise the whole drawing is a quiet wireframe.

rules.name: The Serif Means Source Rule
rules.body: The serif is for text quoted from a source document (the evidence paper) and the landing page's headline. Titles, figures, buttons, navigation, tables and forms stay in Geist.

rules.name: The Mono Means Data Rule
rules.body: Mono is for IDs, labels and state. Never set a sentence of prose in mono for a "technical" feel.

rules.name: The Flat Card Rule
rules.body: Cards and stat tiles take a hairline, never a shadow. Nothing inside a card takes a shadow. Never stack a card on a card.

dos: read every colour from the tokens (`var(--hi)`, `var(--accent)`, `var(--text)`, …); both themes depend on it.
use amber for exactly one meaning: a person must act (see The One Signal Rule).
give anything that waits on a person the needs-you shape as well as the colour.
keep text at 13px or larger and at ≥4.5:1 contrast in both themes.
set titles and figures in Geist, IDs and state in the mono face, and keep the serif for quoted source text.
let wide tables scroll inside their frame, with the edge shadow cue.
donts: use amber for anything that doesn't wait on a person: not branding, not "running", not hover.
use brand orange anywhere but the logo apex and the landing animation.
put shadows on cards, tables, wells or inputs, or stack cards.
round markers: dots, steps and segments are square.
use emoji as icons or status markers; draw icons in the shared stroke family. (The ✎ on "Proposed" is a text glyph, not an icon.)
hard-code colours or fonts in components (third-party editors included); follow the live theme.
fade disabled or switched-off items with opacity; mark them with the well fill or a dashed edge and keep text legible.
